CausalChain: Hypoxia → HIF activation → Upregulation of glycolytic enzymes (LDHA, MCT4) → Elevated lactate production and secretion → Lactate accumulation in tumor microenvironment → Paracrine activation of lactate-sensing pathways in hepatic stellate cells → Differentiation into cancer-associated fibroblasts → Secretion of pro-tumorigenic factors → Enhanced tumor growth, angiogenesis, and drug resistance
Hypothesis: In hypoxic hepatocellular carcinoma, lactate secreted by tumor cells reprograms adjacent hepatic stellate cells into cancer-associated fibroblasts, thus establishing a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment that promotes drug resistance; consequently, inhibition of lactate export (e.g., targeting MCT4) may disrupt this stromal reprogramming and improve the efficacy of existing therapies.
Abstract: This hypothesis posits that under hypoxic conditions in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), HIF‐driven metabolic reprogramming leads to excessive lactate production via upregulation of LDHA and MCT4. This excess lactate, beyond its known roles in immune suppression, acts as a paracrine signal to reprogram neighboring hepatic stellate cells into cancer‐associated fibroblasts (CAFs). The resulting CAFs then secrete growth factors, cytokines, and matrix‐modifying enzymes that further enhance tumor progression and drug resistance. Therefore, disrupting lactate export may not only normalize the tumor microenvironment but also interrupt harmful tumor-stromal cross-talk, thereby sensitizing hypoxic HCC to conventional therapies such as tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs).
